newsitem.title: UK: Gene project could transform views of illness.
newsitem.headline: Gene project could transform views of illness.

text.p: A bid to map all human genes and pinpoint the genetic cause of illnesses like cancer and heart disease could lead to people halting efforts to make themselves healthier, a top scientist said on Monday.

Without tight controls, genetic screening could also lead to dramatic changes in the way people deal with the ill, with family and doctors offering more sympathy but less treatment, she told Britain's main science festival.
Scientists around the world are trying to map all the genes in the body as part of the so-called Human Genome Project.
The mammoth task has already produced huge advances in working out the genetic influences involved in sicknesses like breast and colon cancer, heart disease and diabetes.
But Professor Theresa Marteau, a researcher in psychology and genetics at London's Guy's Hospital, said identifying the genetic cause of diseases could have unexpected social effects.
"This will change how all of us think about disease," said Marteau, one of a group of top scientists studying the link between the mind and the body in illness.
Showing something like heart disease -- a key target of government health programmes -- had a genetic component could make people believe it was "uncontrollable", she said.
"It is likely to lead to a lowering of motivation to alter lifestyle to reduce risk," she added.
Other people, for example mothers told of the risk of genetic disabilities to their unborn children, could face anger and blame if they went ahead and gave birth, she said.
Marteau said more research had to be done to prevent these kind of effects, and restrictions on genetic screening and strict guidelines on their use were essential.
Backing up Marteau, other scientists warned that the way patients feel about themselves can determine their chances for survival in illnesses like heart disease.
Professor Andrew Steptoe of St George's Hospital in London, said people who were confident and had emotional support after operations like open heart surgery were more likely to survive.
As a result doctors and researchers had to look at social and practical matters affecting patients as well as clinical matters like drug levels and blood pressure.
